content: The authors defined the duration of breastfeeding as the period from birth during which the child was at least partially breastfed, regardless of whether bottle supplementation was used. In the Tehran Lipid and Glucose Study (TLGS), a prospective cohort study initiated in 1998 to assess the prevalence of non-communicable disease risk factors, 4028 women aged 15–50 years without metabolic syndrome were identified. From this group, 925 women were randomly selected and followed for nine years. Participants completed a lactation questionnaire and were categorized into five groups based on their lifetime breastfeeding duration: none, 1–6 months, 7–12 months, 13–23 months, and 24 months or more. In a case-control study by Tryggvadottir (2001), data were collected from 80,219 women who participated in Iceland’s nationwide cancer screening program between 1979 and 1995. Women diagnosed with their first invasive breast cancer during this period were identified, and only those who had provided reproductive and menstrual information before their diagnosis were included. For each of the 993 cases, 10 controls were matched by birth year and age at the time of data collection. Breastfeeding duration was categorized into 0–4 weeks, 5–26 weeks, 27–52 weeks, 53–104 weeks, and ≥105 weeks. In a cross-sectional study conducted by Vafa (2012), data were collected in 2008 from seven-year-old children in Tehran. Schools were randomly selected from each of the city’s 19 educational districts, and first-grade students were randomly chosen. Exclusion criteria included twins and children with specific diseases. Mothers provided information on infant feeding practices, birth weight, birth order, and parental characteristics. Breastfeeding duration and cessation age were recorded. Child weight status was assessed using the 2007 WHO growth reference. In a study by Vazquez-Nava (2008), children from the Tampico-Madero-Altamira area in Mexico were included as part of a larger multidisciplinary research project. Data on feeding practices during the first year of life were collected using validated questionnaires. Physical examinations were conducted as part of routine nursery healthcare activities. The Mysore Parthenon Study (Veena, 2010) was a prospective birth cohort study initiated in 1997–1998. Breastfeeding duration was categorized into six groups: <3 months, 3–5 months, 6–8 months, 9–11 months, 12–17 months, and ≥18 months. Cognitive function was assessed using various standardized tests, including the Atlantis, Word Order, Pattern Reasoning, Verbal Fluency, Kohs Block Design, and Coding-WISC III. In a cross-sectional study by Vehapoglu (2017), 5000 Turkish children aged 2–14 years were recruited from outpatient clinics in Istanbul between June 2012 and July 2014. Children born before 38 weeks of gestation, with low birth weight, congenital defects, or long-term diseases, were excluded. Breastfeeding duration and the introduction of formula or solid foods were recorded. Feeding groups were classified as breastfed for ≤6 months, 7–12 months, and 13–24 months. Outcomes included underweight, normal weight, overweight, and obesity based on BMI percentiles. In a study conducted in Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil, data were collected from two districts with approximately 140,000 inhabitants each. Mothers or close relatives provided information on breastfeeding duration. Breastfeeding duration was categorized into <3 months, 3–5 months, 6–8 months, 9–11 months, and ≥18 months. The Tanzania Vitamin A Study (Villamor, 2000) was a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial conducted between 1993 and 1997 among 687 children aged 6–60 months admitted with pneumonia to Muhimbili Medical Center in Dar es Salaam. A cross-sectional analysis of 161 children examined the relationships between anemia, baseline hemoglobin concentration, socioeconomic status, malaria, HIV diagnoses, breastfeeding, and nutritional status. In a retrospective cohort study by Walby (2016), infants born between 2002 and 2007 in two Swedish counties were studied. Children with missing or out-of-range growth data or incomplete breastfeeding information were excluded. Breastfeeding data were collected at various time points during the first year of life. The Calex family study (Wiklund, 2012) was conducted in Jyväskylä, Finland, as part of a retrospective cohort study. Breastfeeding duration and its relationship to various health outcomes were analyzed.
